# Battle of Huayang

King Zhaoxiang of Qin reigned for 56 years, making him the longest-reigning monarch in the history of the State of Qin. Under his rule, Qin became the most powerful state during the Warring States period of the Eastern Zhou dynasty, actively engaging in wars of expansion and accelerating the process of annexing the other six states. In 280 BC, Qin captured Qianzhong from the State of Chu through Sima Cuo, forcing Chu to cede Shangyong and the region north of the Han River. Subsequently, Bai Qi captured Yancheng and Ying (the Chu capital), forcing King Qingxiang of Chu to flee and move the capital to Chen. After the temporary conclusion of the Qin-Chu conflict, Qin turned its attention toward the State of Wei. In 275 BC, Wei Ran decisively defeated the Wei army, forcing Wei to cede eight cities for peace.
The Battle of Huayang in 273 BC saw the Qin forces, led by Wei Ran, Bai Qi, and Hu Yang, achieve a major victory over the allied forces of Zhao and Wei, decapitating 150,000 troops and forcing Wei to cede Nanyang. This is considered one of Bai Qi's four greatest military victories, alongside the Battle of Yique, the Battle of Yan-Ying, and the Battle of Changping. Following the battle, the State of Wei was severely weakened and submitted completely to Qin. Simultaneously, Qin paused its expansion to restore friendly relations with Chu, further solidifying its dominance. While the Battle of Yique led to significant territorial gains in Wan, Nanyang, and eastern Wei, the territorial changes following the Battle of Huayang were less extensive because the lands of Han and Wei had already been significantly reduced.

Background
In 280 BC, Qin resumed its offensive against the State of Chu. Sima Cuo led troops from Longxi and Shu to capture Qianzhong. King Qingxiang of Chu was forced to cede Shangyong and the lands north of the Han River to Qin.
In 279 BC, King Zhaoxiang dispatched Bai Qi to lead a southern campaign. He quickly occupied Deng (present-day Xiangyang) and approached Yancheng (present-day Yicheng), the northern gateway to Chu. Bai Qi famously used a water-diversion tactic to flood and destroy the city.
In 278 BC, Bai Qi continued his advance, capturing the capital Ying, seizing Yiling (where he burned the tombs of Chu's former kings), and occupying Jingling. King Qingxiang fled northeast and moved the capital to Chen (present-day Huaiyang, Henan). Qin established the South Prefecture (Nanjun) at Ying, and Bai Qi was titled the "Lord of Wu'an" (Wu'an Jun) for his achievements. With the Qin-Chu war stabilized, Qin shifted its expansion toward the Central Plains, targeting Han and Wei. In 276 BC, Bai Qi led troops against Wei and captured two cities, marking the start of a major conflict in the Central Plains.
In 275 BC, the Qin Chancellor Wei Ran attacked Wei and reached its capital, Daliang. King Anxi of Wei sought help from Han. The King of Han appointed Bao Yuan as commander to rescue Wei. However, Wei Ran defeated the Han army, killing 40,000 troops. Wei was forced to cede eight cities. Wei Ran then defeated the Wei general Mang Mao and besieged Daliang. The Wei official Xu Jia successfully persuaded Wei Ran to accept the cession of Wenyu (present-day Wen County) in exchange for lifting the siege.
The Battle of Huayang
The Battle of Huayang took place in 273 BC between the State of Qin and the allied forces of Wei and Zhao.
In 273 BC, Zhao and Wei launched a joint attack on the State of Han, nearing the strategic city of Huayang. King Xi of Han sent an envoy to Qin to beg for aid, but King Zhaoxiang was initially reluctant. The Han Chancellor then summoned the strategist Tian Ling (also known as Chen Shi) to go to Xianyang.
When Chen Shi met Wei Ran, the Chancellor asked arrogantly, "Is the situation urgent? Is that why you have come?" Chen Shi replied, "Not yet." Outraged, Wei Ran asked why he claimed it wasn't urgent if Han was under siege. Chen Shi explained, "If the situation were truly desperate, Han would have already defected to another side. Because we still rely on Qin, I say it is not yet urgent." Realizing that Qin might lose an ally, Wei Ran immediately ordered the mobilization of troops.
King Zhaoxiang then dispatched Wei Ran, Bai Qi, and the guest official Hu Yang to rescue Han. The Qin army utilized a surprise tactic, conducting a long-distance forced march at a speed of a hundred li per day. After eight days, the Qin army suddenly appeared at the Huayang battlefield and caught the Zhao-Wei alliance off guard. Qin crushed the allied forces, decapitating 130,000 Wei soldiers and capturing three generals. The Wei commander Mang Mao fled, and the Zhao general Jia Yan was defeated, leading to 20,000 of his soldiers drowning in the Yellow River.
Qin seized several cities from Wei, including Juan, Caiyang, and Changshe, as well as Guanjin from Zhao. This forced Wei to sue for peace by ceding the Nanyang region.
Aftermath
Following the Battle of Huayang, both Han and Wei were forced into submission. King Zhaoxiang turned his attention toward the states of Qi and Chu. He ordered Wei Ran to return Guanjin to Zhao to facilitate a joint attack on Qi and commanded Bai Qi to prepare an offensive against Chu.
Upon hearing of Qin's plans to attack Qi, King Xiang of Qi sent Su Dai to secretly persuade Wei Ran to withdraw. Su Dai argued that Qin should focus on consolidating its current holdings rather than overextending into Qi. Wei Ran accepted this advice and retreated.
Meanwhile, the Chu envoy Huang Xie (the future Lord Chunshen) arrived in Xianyang. Fearing a Qin invasion, he submitted a memorial to King Zhaoxiang, arguing that a war between the "two tigers" (Qin and Chu) would only benefit Han and Wei. King Zhaoxiang agreed, halted Bai Qi's advance, and established a "friendly state" alliance with Chu. In 272 BC, King Qingxiang of Chu sent Crown Prince Xiong Wan to Qin as a hostage, with Huang Xie accompanying him as an advisor. For the next decade, Qin and Chu maintained a period of relative peace.
